The instanceof operator in PHP also returns true if an object implements a specific interface.
In PHP, interface methods cannot have a body or default implementation; they are abstract by definition.

In PHP 7 and later, TypeError extends Error, not Exception, so it will not be caught by a catch (Exception $e) block.
The @ operator suppresses errors and warnings, not exceptions; exceptions must be caught with try-catch blocks.
The intdiv() function throws a DivisionByZeroError when the divisor is zero.

Casting a non-null object (including an Exception instance) to bool always returns true in PHP.
Functions registered with register_shutdown_function() are executed when the script execution finishes, which includes normal completion, calling exit/die, or an uncaught fatal error.

The use statement is purely a syntactic alias that maps a fully qualified class name to a shorter local name; it does not trigger the autoloader or load the class file until the class is actually instantiated or used.

In PHP's `use` statements, functions are imported using the `function` keyword and constants using the `const` keyword, so the word that follows `use` to import a constant (not a function or class) is `const`.
PSR-4 converts the namespace App\Controller\Api into the directory path Controller/Api and appends the class name with .php.
The autoload.php file generated by Composer calls spl_autoload_register() to register its custom autoloader.
The magic constant __NAMESPACE__ indeed returns the name of the current namespace at compile time.
Unqualified class names in new are resolved from the current namespace, not the global root.
PSR-4 autoloading maps the namespace hierarchy 'App\Model\User' to the directory structure relative to the root path, resulting in src/Model/User.php.
In PHP, use statements for namespacing or functions can be declared inside a function scope, limiting their effect to that function only.
In PHP, arrays are value types and are copied by value on assignment, so modifying one variable does not affect the other unless reference semantics are explicitly used.
PHP arrays are passed by value (copy-on-write), so modifying $b does not affect $a; $a still has 2 elements.

In PHP, variables defined outside a function have global scope and are not directly accessible inside a function unless brought into scope via the global statement, the $GLOBALS superglobal array, or passed as parameters.
The $GLOBALS array is a reference to the global symbol table, so unsetting an element removes the variable from the entire global scope, not just the local function scope.
The parameter &$x indicates pass-by-reference, so modifying $x increments $n directly.
A foreach loop in PHP creates a copy of the array (by default) and iterates over that copy, so modifications to the original array do not affect the iteration in the current pass.
Static properties are shared among all instances of a class, so changes in one object are visible in others.
Array keys in PHP are stored as integers or strings, so the boolean value true is automatically cast to the integer key 1.

In PHP generators, returning a value (e.g., return $value) sets the return value of the generator, which can be retrieved by calling getReturn() on the Generator object after it has been fully iterated.
In PHP, the rewind() method can be used on a Generator object that has been fully consumed to restart its execution from the beginning.
The yield from construct in PHP allows a generator to delegate to another iterable or generator, effectively yielding values from the sub-iterable.
A function containing a yield statement returns a Generator object, and get_class() returns the string "Generator" for such instances.
The generator yields three elements (1, 2, 3), so iterator_to_array produces an array with 3 items.
The SplStack class implements a LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) queue, not FIFO (First-In, First-Out).
ArrayIterator is a built-in PHP class that implements the Iterator interface, allowing you to wrap an array and iterate over its elements using foreach or explicit iterator methods.
ArrayObject implements the Traversable interface, so it can be iterated with foreach.
The password_hash() function in PHP automatically generates a unique salt and embeds it in the returned hash string.
PASSWORD_DEFAULT currently uses the bcrypt algorithm (specifically $2y$), not MD5.
password_verify compares the plaintext password with the hash generated by password_hash using the same algorithm, returning true.
strip_tags removes HTML/XML tags but does not protect against SQL injection; prepared statements or escaping are required for that.
session_regenerate_id() creates a new session ID, which is the standard method for preventing session fixation attacks by invalidating the previous ID after privilege changes like login.
The built-in function php_sapi_name() returns the name of the current SAPI (Server API) interface, such as 'cli' for command-line or 'apache2' for web servers.
session_destroy() only removes the session data stored on the server; the session ID cookie remains in the user's browser unless manually unset.
Session data is not automatically loaded into $_SESSION until session_start() is called to initialize the session.
The array_find() function was introduced in PHP 8.3.0 along with other new array functions.
PHP 8.4 introduced property hooks, allowing getters and setters to be defined directly within a property declaration.
Asymmetric visibility was introduced in PHP 8.1, not 8.4.
The #[\NoDiscard] attribute was introduced in PHP 8.4 to enforce the use of return values.
PHP 8.4 introduced the pipe operator (|>) as part of the DNF types and other new features.
Clone with arguments (clone-with) was introduced in PHP 8.4.
The array_first() and array_last() functions were introduced in PHP 8.4.
RFC Partial Function Application v2 was adopted for PHP 8.4, introducing the fn keyword for partial application.
The clamp() function was introduced in PHP 8.4 as part of the RFC clamp_v2.

The RFC for Native Implementations of Generics (RFC 5549) was accepted in 2024 and implemented in PHP 8.4, not declined in 2026.

As of 2026, PHP still uses standard builds by default; the RFC to make the Zend Thread Safety (ZTS) build the default has not been accepted in recent PHP versions (such as 8.4 or anticipated 9.0), though the debate has been ongoing for years.

PHP has not implemented native generics or parameterized types in any version up to PHP 8.4 (the current stable major version as of early 2025), and PHP 8.5 is not yet released; the language continues to rely on static analysis tools and array conventions for type safety.
PHP 8.5 was released on November 21, 2024, not 2026.
PHP 6 was a development branch that was abandoned and replaced directly by PHP 7.0.

The RFC to add a #[\Deprecated] attribute to the PHP core has not been adopted; it has been rejected in favor of other approaches or is still pending/not accepted as of the current stable PHP versions.
In clean and onion architectures, business logic (the core) is independent of details, so dependencies must point inward from outer layers to the center.

In a well-structured Domain-Driven Design (DDD) architecture, domain entities should be pure PHP classes that depend only on the language core and standard library, remaining agnostic to frameworks like Doctrine or Symfony.
Controllers and Twig templates are part of the Presentation Layer, not the Business-Logic Layer, as they handle request/response and view rendering.
In onion architecture, the Core (or Domain) layer sits at the center, depending on nothing else.
Tools like Deptrac analyze static code to detect violations of defined layer dependencies and can fail the build if forbidden calls are found.
Use cases should be decoupled from specific frameworks like HTTP or Doctrine EntityManager to maintain testability and flexibility.

In Domain-Driven Design and PHP frameworks like Doctrine, the Repository pattern acts as an in-memory collection of domain objects that hides the specific data source or storage mechanism behind an abstract interface.
In Clean Architecture, database adapters are infrastructure entities that implement repository interfaces, allowing the domain and use cases to remain independent of specific technology choices.
An aggregate in DDD is a cluster of domain objects treated as a unit for data changes, not simply a database table.
By definition, a Value Object is immutable and equality is determined by comparing its internal state (fields) rather than object identity (memory address).
In Domain-Driven Design, the Aggregate Root is the designated entry point for an aggregate, ensuring consistency and handling all changes to the aggregate.
In Domain-Driven Design, repositories are defined at the aggregate root level to maintain transactional consistency and enforce invariant boundaries.
Ubiquitous language in Domain-Driven Design is a shared language used by both developers and domain experts to ensure the model and business concepts are clearly aligned.
In software architecture, an umbrella is a boundary that provides consistent terminology and understanding for the people involved in the system.
DDD recommends rich domain models where business logic resides within the domain entities and value objects, not in anemic models with logic in services.

In Domain-Driven Design, each bounded context has its own model, meaning the same real-world concept can be represented by different classes with different attributes and behaviors in different contexts.
Symfony's DependencyInjection container instantiates services only when they are first requested, rather than at boot time.
The `debug:router` command is used to list all registered routes in a Symfony application.
Symfony autowiring automatically resolves dependencies by type-hinting, so services do not need to be manually declared in services.yaml if they can be autoconfigured.
Twig compiles templates into PHP files/classes and caches them to improve performance and avoid recompilation on every request.

In the Symfony dev environment, the DI container is typically rebuilt on every request (unless cached via warmup or specific opcache settings), whereas the prod environment is static and only rebuilt manually.
The APP_ENV environment variable is used to specify the active Symfony environment, such as 'dev' or 'prod'.
Symfony routing requires controller methods to be public, as the framework invokes them via reflection and expects public visibility.
Both event subscribers and listeners have a priority, but subscribers do not inherently receive events before listeners.
Symfony 5.3 introduced the new security system based on authenticator classes, and the legacy Guard system was deprecated in 5.4 and removed in Symfony 6.0.
The #IsGranted attribute in Symfony checks if the current user has the specified role or permission, returning a 403 error if not.
Symfony uses the Voter system (Voters) to implement object-level access control via the isGranted() method with a subject argument.

Doctrine Annotations are deprecated in Symfony 6.0 but still supported in Symfony 7.0 (with a deprecation warning); native PHP attributes are the recommended way, but annotations are not completely removed in 7.0, only scheduled for removal in 8.0.
Symfony's form component automatically adds a CSRF token field to forms and validates it during submission unless explicitly disabled.
Client-side validation is for user experience, while server-side validation ensures data integrity and security, so both must pass in Symfony.
The Symfony MakerBundle command to generate a FormType class is 'make:form'.
Symfony stores hashed passwords in the database, not in the session, and never stores plain-text passwords.
In modern Symfony applications (4.0+), bundle configuration is indeed organized in the config/packages directory, with one file per bundle (e.g., framework.yaml, security.yaml).
This is a common best practice where .env (or .env.example) containing safe defaults is committed, while .env.local contains sensitive secrets and is ignored by version control.
The Symfony console command debug:container is used to inspect the service container, listing services and aliases.
The Symfony container is compiled and immutable at runtime; parameters cannot be changed with setParameter() after compilation.
Since Symfony 4.3, services are private (public: false) by default to improve performance and allow for better optimizations.
In Symfony, a bundle does not require a configuration file in config/packages to function; many bundles work with default configurations or no configuration at all.
Symfony's service container supports injecting environment variables into services.yaml (or config files) using the %env(VAR_NAME)% placeholder syntax.

The environment where debug is enabled is typically defined by APP_ENV=dev in .env.local or via the APP_DEBUG=true variable, but the question asks which variable enables debug mode; the correct answer is APP_DEBUG.
Symfony Messenger allows multiple handlers to be associated with a single message; the framework iterates through them in order of priority or as a chain.
The sync transport processes the message immediately in the same process, whereas async transports queue it for a separate worker process.
The Symfony console command to start a worker that processes Messenger queue messages is 'bin/console messenger:consume'.
In Symfony Messenger, retry strategies are configured globally or via message middleware (e.g., `retry` middleware), not directly per transport definition in the configuration file.
Symfony Messenger uses a JSON serializer by default for message serialization.

Symfony Scheduler is a standalone component for scheduling and triggering PHP functions, whereas Symfony Messenger is a separate component for handling asynchronous message processing and queues; while they can be integrated, the Scheduler does not inherently dispatch through the Messenger bus by de
The doctrine transport in Symfony Messenger persists messages in database tables managed by Doctrine DBAL or ORM.
Laravel's Messenger pipeline allows adding custom middleware to the beginning or end of the middleware stack.
Symfony releases major versions every two years (even-numbered years) and LTS versions every four years, with minor updates typically in May and November.
Symfony 8 (like Symfony 7) requires PHP 8.4 or higher as its minimum version.
Symfony 7.0 maintains support for docblock attributes (annotations) for features like routing and validation, even though PHP 8 native attributes are preferred.
AssetMapper in Symfony 7+ replaces the old Asset component with a new system that uses importmap.php to manage CSS and JS assets without requiring Node.js or Webpack.

When upgrading to a new major version in Symfony, all deprecations from the previous version are removed and are no longer supported.

The Symfony AssetMapper component, introduced in Symfony 6.4, manages JavaScript and CSS assets and integrates with the Importmap component to handle dependencies without requiring Node.js or a bundler like Webpack.
Symfony 8.2 is scheduled for release in November 2026.
Symfony versions increment by 0.1 for each subsequent minor release within the same major version.

Symfony follows semantic versioning where major releases (e.g., 8.0) may introduce breaking changes, but 8.2 is a minor release of the 8.x line, which maintains backward compatibility with the 8.0 API.
In PHP, backward compatibility is generally maintained across minor versions within a major release, so updating from 8.1 to 8.2 should not require code changes for most applications.
Symfony 8.4 is the final minor release in the 8.x branch before the introduction of Symfony 9.0.

Symfony's policy guarantees that features deprecated in the 8.x branch will be maintained until the 9.0 release, at which point they are removed.
Twig does not allow calling arbitrary PHP code directly inside the {{ }} syntax; it only supports template-specific expressions and functions.
Twig has auto-escaping enabled by default to prevent XSS attacks.
The |e filter in Twig automatically escapes strings for safe output in an HTML context by default.
The number_format filter in the intl-extra package uses PHP's NumberFormatter to format numbers according to the specified locale.

In Symfony templates, the raw filter is not a standard built-in filter, and Twig's default is that |raw marks a string as already escaped, but there is no general |raw filter for disabling auto-escaping in the way described.
In Twig, double curly braces ({{ }}) are used for outputting variables or expressions, while percent signs ({% %}) are used for control structures like loops, conditions, and variable assignment.
Twig allows declaring variables within a template using the 'set' tag (e.g., {% set foo = 'bar' %}).
The dump function in Twig is used to dump a variable's structure, similar to var_dump in PHP.
Bootstrap is primarily a front-end framework for building responsive user interfaces with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, not a single-page application (SPA) framework like React or Angular.
The 'container' class provides a responsive fixed-width container that adjusts its max-width based on the current breakpoint.
The Bootstrap grid actually uses CSS flexbox and splits a row into 12 columns.
Bootstrap 5 defines five named breakpoints: sm, md, lg, xl, and xxl.

In Bootstrap, utilities like .mt-3 or .px-2 use a predefined spacing scale where each step is a multiple of $spacer, but the specific values depend on the $spacing variable and the scale, not just simple multiples of $spacer without context.
The data-bs-toggle attribute is used in Bootstrap 5 to trigger interactive components like dropdowns, popovers, and tooltips.
Bootstrap 5 dropped its dependency on jQuery in favor of using vanilla JavaScript.
In Bootstrap 5, dark mode is enabled by adding the data-bs-theme="dark" attribute to the <html> element, not a .dark class.
Doctrine ORM does not automatically create tables; you must explicitly use a migration tool like Doctrine Migrations or the ORM Tools setup-database tool.
The persist() method in Doctrine's EntityManager makes an entity managed and schedules an INSERT statement to be executed upon flush().
EntityManager::merge() copies the state of a detached entity to its managed counterpart (creating it if necessary) and returns the managed instance, effectively making the object managed.
DQL (Doctrine Query Language) is an object-oriented query language that maps to entities and their fields, abstracting the underlying database tables and columns.
In Doctrine ORM, if no entity is found, the repository's find method returns null.

By default, Symfony's DoctrineBundle does not automatically call flush() at the end of every request; persistence is only triggered if the 'auto_commit' option is enabled in the ORM configuration, which is false by default to allow explicit control.
For entities already managed by the Entity Manager, the Unit of Work automatically tracks changes, so flush() will commit them without needing an explicit persist() call.
In Doctrine ORM, remove() only marks the entity for deletion in the UnitOfWork; the actual SQL DELETE is issued when flush() is called.
In PostgreSQL's MVCC, readers do not block writers and writers do not block readers, allowing high concurrency.
The EXPLAIN command displays the query execution plan without running the query.
SERIAL is a PostgreSQL-specific convenience feature that creates a sequence and a column, while IDENTITY columns are a standard SQL 2003 feature with different behaviors and syntax.
In PostgreSQL, by default, a UNIQUE constraint treats NULL values as distinct from each other, allowing multiple rows with NULL in the constrained column.
The string_agg function in PostgreSQL concatenates string values with a specified separator.
Plain VACUUM marks the space as reusable within the database file but does not shrink the file; only VACUUM FULL reclaims space from the operating system.
The PARTITION BY clause divides rows into groups for window functions to operate over independently.
The READ COMMITTED isolation level protects against dirty reads but does not prevent non-repeatable reads.

By default, PostgreSQL operates in autocommit mode, where every single SQL statement is automatically wrapped in its own transaction that commits immediately upon success unless explicitly placed within a BEGIN...COMMIT block.
COMMIT is the SQL command used to finalize and save all changes made during a transaction.
Database indexes improve the performance of UPDATE and DELETE operations by helping the database quickly locate the specific rows to modify or remove, especially when filtering conditions are used.
SAVEPOINT in PostgreSQL allows for partial rollback of a transaction by rolling back to a specific point within it.
EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query to gather actual performance statistics, whereas plain EXPLAIN only displays the plan without execution.
pgvector is a PostgreSQL extension that adds vector types and indexes, specifically for handling embeddings.
PHP does not support the SQL syntax for creating partial indexes (CREATE INDEX ... WHERE ...), as this is a database-specific feature, not a PHP language feature.

PostgreSQL implements SERIALIZABLE isolation using Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI), which detects conflicts at commit time rather than by locking all read rows like the READ COMMITTED or REPEATABLE READ levels.
HTTP status 201 indicates that the request has been fulfilled and has resulted in one or more new resources being created.
HTTP status code 204 (No Content) indicates that the server has successfully processed the request but is not returning any content in the response body.
The HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 specifications explicitly define the DELETE method as idempotent, meaning that multiple identical requests should have the same effect as a single request.
The Access-Control-Allow-Origin header is sent by the server, not the client.
HTTP status code 429 specifically indicates that the user has sent too many requests in a given amount of time.
HTTP 4xx codes indicate client errors, while 5xx codes indicate server errors.
The Content-Type header specifies the media type (MIME type) of the resource.
RFC 5789 explicitly states that the PATCH method is not required to be idempotent, whereas PUT is designed to be idempotent.
Using == allows type juggling which can cause false positives, so strict === comparison should be used.
CSRF tokens are indeed issued by the server and validated on the server side during state-changing requests to ensure authenticity.
The HTTP header used to define a Content Security Policy is 'Content-Security-Policy'.

OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework that grants delegated access, not primarily an authentication protocol, and access tokens are opaque strings that do not inherently identify the user without additional claims (as in OpenID Connect).
XSS (Cross-Site Scripting) is primarily prevented by encoding output when rendering it to the browser, not just by validating input on the server or storing it in the database.

In the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, the authorization server redirects the user agent back to the client's redirect_uri with a temporary authorization code, which the client then exchanges for an access token.
Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials used to obtain new access tokens without requiring user re-authentication.
A salt is stored alongside the hash (typically in the database) to allow verification; it does not need to be kept secret, only unique per user.
In PHPUnit, test classes must extend PHPUnit\Framework\TestCase (or a descendant) to be recognized and executed as test suites.
setUp() runs before every test method, while setUpBeforeClass() runs once before all tests.
A data provider yields a single set of arguments for one specific execution of a test method.
The expectException method in PHPUnit is used to declare an expectation that an exception of the specified class will be thrown during test execution.
The statement is reversed: stubs only return data, while mocks verify methods were called.
PHPUnit 10 supports PHP attributes, and while annotations still work, attributes are the modern, recommended syntax.
PHPUnit provides the @depends annotation and the dependency() method specifically to allow one test to depend on the data or result of another test.
The --random-order flag in PHPUnit instructs the test runner to execute tests in a randomized sequence.
intdiv(7,2) returns 3 and intdiv(-7,2) returns -4 (rounds towards negative infinity), concatenated to '3-4'.
The exponentiation operator ** has higher precedence than the unary minus, so it evaluates as -(3 ** 2), which is -9.
In PHP 7, both strings are converted to numbers; 1e1 is 10 and 10 is 10, so they are equal.
In PHP, 'a' is not loose-equal to 0, so the default case is executed, outputting 'other'.
strtr with an array replaces the longest matching key first, so 'ab' is replaced by '2' and the remaining 'c' stays, resulting in '2bc'.
substr() with a negative offset of -10 on a 5-character string starts before the string, so it returns the entire string 'hello'.
The array union operator (+) combines arrays by keys, with the left array taking precedence for duplicate keys; array_keys returns the resulting keys in order, which are k, n, and m.

The usort sorts the array by the third element (index 2) in ascending order, resulting in the order of second elements ('x', 'z', 'y') becoming 'y', 'z', 'x' after sorting by the third element values 1, 2, 2, then implode concatenates them.
PHP 8.1+ allows spreading an array with named keys into a function call, matching arguments by name; thus $a=5 and $b=1, resulting in 5-1=4.
The closure $f binds to the object $p via $this, so even after $p is set to null, the closure keeps the object alive and $this->v is still 3.
The `static::class` keyword returns the name of the late-bound calling class, which is B in this case.
The property $x is initialized to 0. When $c->x = 5 is executed, the setter is called, which sets $this->x to 5 * 2 = 10. Thus, echo $c->x outputs 10.
The `insteadof` operator makes `TB::f` the primary `f` method (returning 'B'), and `TA::f as g` aliases the TA version as `g` (returning 'A').
Static properties defined in a trait are separate for each class using the trait, so changing CX::$n does not affect CY::$n.
In PHP, a return in the finally block overrides the return value from the try block.
The finally block throws a LogicException which suppresses the original RuntimeException, and this new exception is caught by the outer catch block.
Baz is aliased to App\Foo, and \Baz resolves to the current namespace N, forming N\Baz.
